description: Groundwork aims to use Earth observation data to better understand and address real-world challenges. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we're exploring how NASA data can help farmers make more informed decisions and adapt to changing environmental conditions.
summary:
Groundwork is a web application that uses NASA Earth data to help Ohio farmers understand how their crop rotations affect their soil's exposure to rainfall.

Many Ohio farmers alternate between corn and soybeans, leaving their fields without living crops for much of the year. Rainfall during these months increases the risk of soil erosion and nutrient runoff into nearby waterways. 

Groundwork helps farmers explore alternative planting strategies while considering the potential benefits, costs, and risks involved.
details:
Groundwork

Is your soil bare when the rain comes?

Project Links

Live App: https://groundwork-d21p.onrender.com

GitHub: https://github.com/n-h-a/groundwork

Slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1mozUACUqG7LXbw_3f2q_CAYFAdUKMzFka5C0oBNAZ9I/edit?usp=sharing

Why I Built It

I recently moved to Ohio and wanted to learn more about the land and communities around me. As I learned about the importance of agriculture and the environmental challenges farmers face, I wanted to create something useful for my new community.

My goal was to build a tool that helps farmers make informed decisions about their own fields while supporting the long term health of Ohio's soil and waterways.

I also wanted Groundwork to feel approachable to the farmers using it. I chose a bright background, readable fonts, and a clean layout to make the information easier to navigate and understand, especially when outdoors!

What Groundwork Does

Farmers select their field on an interactive map and answer a few questions about their farming practices.

The application has four sections:

1. My Field: Shows historical crops since 2008, winter vegetation observed by satellite, and rainfall exposure during months without living crops.

2. Compare: Compares corn and soybean rotations with alternatives that include winter wheat and red clover. It shows changes in rainfall exposure alongside agricultural research about potential benefits and risks.

3. Weather: Displays historical precipitation, temperature patterns, extreme weather trends, and conditions during sensitive crop growth periods.

4. How It Works: Explains the data sources, calculations, research evidence, and limitations behind the results.

How It Works Using NASA Data

Groundwork combines two NASA datasets with USDA agricultural records.

NASA POWER: Provides 35 years of historical precipitation and temperature data. Groundwork uses this information with typical crop calendars to calculate bare-soil rain, the average precipitation falling during months without living crops.

NASA MODIS: Uses satellite observations to measure winter vegetation greenness, helping farmers understand historical vegetation patterns.

USDA Cropland Data Layer: Identifies which crops historically grew at the selected location.

Groundwork also uses published agricultural research to explain potential advantages and disadvantages of different rotations. It checks whether the conditions of research studies match the farmer's practices and flags findings that may not apply.

Example Results

For an example field west of Dayton, Ohio, Groundwork calculated the following average annual precipitation during months without living crops:

  • Corn and soybeans: 27.1 inches
  • Adding winter wheat: 22.3 inches
  • Adding winter wheat and red clover: 12.9 inches

Adding winter wheat and red clover reduced the modeled rainfall exposure by approximately 52% compared with the traditional rotation.

These estimates measure precipitation exposure, rather than actual erosion or nutrient loss.

Impact and Future Goals

Groundwork makes NASA's environmental data more accessible to farmers and helps them evaluate planting decisions using information relevant to their own land.

I hope to expand the application beyond Ohio and incorporate additional information, including soil types and land slope, to improve its analysis.

Ultimately, I want Groundwork to help farmers protect their land while maintaining productive farms.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

I built Groundwork with assistance from Claude by Anthropic.

I developed the concept, determined the application's features and design direction, contributed code, reviewed the research, and checked the results.

Claude helped find data sources, wrote much of the code and tests, created crop icons, and drafted documentation.

The application itself does not use generative AI. Its calculations rely on NASA and USDA data, crop calendars, and published agricultural research.

References and Tools

NASA POWER: https://power.larc.nasa.gov/

NASA MODIS: https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/mod13q1v061/

USDA Cropland Data Layer: https://www.nass.usda.gov/Research_and_Science/Cropland/SARS1a.php

Agricultural research: 

1. Huo, Frey, Lindsey, Benitez. Yield and soil responses to adding wheat to a corn-soybean rotation. Crop, Forage & Turfgrass Management, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1002/cft2.20143

2. Benefits of incorporating wheat in a three-crop rotation. Ohio's Country Journal, 2020. https://ocj.com/2020/06/benefits-of-incorporating-wheat-in-a-three-crop-rotation/

3. How do cover crops impact field nitrogen and phosphorous losses? Ohio State University C.O.R.N. Newsletter, 2021. https://agcrops.osu.edu/newsletter/corn-newsletter/24-2021/how-do-cover-crops-impact-field-nitrogen-and-phosphorous-losses

4. R.L. Nielsen. Drought and Heat Stress Effects on Corn Pollination. Purdue University. https://www.agry.purdue.edu/ext/corn/pubs/corn-07.htm

5. Irrigating Soybean (G1367). University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension. https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1367/na/html/view

6. Crop Progress, reports released July 20 to August 10, 2026. USDA NASS. https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/release-files/795995/prog3026.pdf

7. Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd edition: Red Clover. SARE, 2007. https://www.sare.org/publications/managing-cover-crops-profitably/legume-cover-crops/red-clover/

8. Remote Sensing, 2021 (NDVI alone is not enough to detect cover crops). https://doi.org/10.3390/rs13101998

Technologies: Python, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, Vite, Recharts, Leaflet, Docker, Render, and Claude.
